We associate the initial investment with a single quantum system's ergotropy - a measure equivalent to the quantum analogue of free energy, as described by Allahverdyan, Balian, and Nieuwenhuizen - and express it through electromagnetic radiation. As betting outcomes occur, this system experiences attenuation and amplification, simulating loss and winning events. This stochastic evolution in the quantum memory is analogous to the random lasing phenomenon and can be characterized in a Bosonic Gaussian channel framework. Furthermore, in a double bet, this model connects to the well-known "roulette" problem in probability theory. We also explain how this model can be implemented using continuous quantum variables and demonstrate that it has a connection to real-world applications such as thermalized lasers and solid-state active memory. Additionally, we explore how double betting can be represented as a two-time quantum evolutions with negative trace, and examine the conditions under which this model can be considered as a quantum communication channel. Lastly, we discuss the difficulties and limitations associated with single and double betting models in the context of quantum mechanics and assess their potential use in further research. This work marks the first integration of the "roulette" problem and related betting issues with quantum mechanics. We have also extended the existing models, integrating the conventional payout concept into the mean-field model for the description of the initial investment. Furthermore, this study offers an innovative approach to the time reversal problem based on the assumption that the system undergoes a time asymmetrical evolution when it experiences attenuation or amplification. This new model for time reversal has potential applications in the description of the system's physical properties and the development of quantum mechanics. Lastly, this study presents an alternative method for the description of the random lasing phenomenon, as well as a new model for quantum memory that is linked to electromagnetic radiation. By incorporating the betting model and the consideration of intrinsic properties of the quantum memory and the payout, we have also developed a unique approach to the description of passive QITs through active QITs. A notable benefit of Transformer models is their ability to capture complex dependencies within input sequences while facilitating parallel processing, an advantage over traditional recurrent networks. Unlike convolutional networks, Transformers rely on minimal inductive biases in their design, making them ideally suited for set-function approximations characteristic of various computer vision tasks. Despite this promising foundation, it remains unclear whether Transformers are effective in various computer vision applications and tasks. To address this knowledge gap, our study investigates the potential of barebones Transformers in solving crucial computer vision challenges, incorporating a training method that leverages hardware-inspired data augmentation to enhance their performance. By applying this approach to challenging CV tasks such as deblurring and demosaicking, we are able to achieve outstanding results, surpassing existing state-of-the-art models in the process. These success stories demonstrate the feasibility of utilizing lightweight Transformers in a wide range of important computer vision applications. Furthermore, our research also includes comprehensive ablation studies to investigate the properties of the proposed data augmentation method as well as the capabilities of the proposed model in various CV tasks, notably in super-resolution, in-painting, and video prediction. Moreover, our novel model can efficiently perform multi-task learning based on the capability of the proposed diffusion model to capture dense features. Following pre-training the transformer on a large image dataset like ImageNet, we found that it is possible to replicate some human vision properties such as focusing on object of interest and filtering out distracting information, incorporating a zooming mechanism in the proposed data augmentation to achieve this goal. Additionally, our study reveals the uniqueness of the points sampled by the proposed demosaicking model, and the ability of the transformer to effectively predict future video frames using a conventional approach, and to perform intricate vision tasks such as image super-resolution, in-painting and video prediction more efficiently and effectively. we minimize the chance of multiple people sharing the same winning ticket.
The results show that our strategy successfully raises the return on a lottery ticket
without increasing the size of the grand prize.
Additionally, we've found the ideal time to maximize earnings from ticket sales.
Interestingly, we've found that our strategy generates profit when the jackpot reaches $500
million or more at a specific point in time, specifically around mid-April for the Mega
Million and around October for the Powerball. Furthermore, we've found the ideal and
minimum bettor participation needed for a high return on a lottery ticket. If
Budweiser Stadium's attendance range is a good indicator ($10,729-$52,612) for a
representative group of people, we recommend a total of 40,000 to 60,000 people
participating in the lottery for optimal results. The proposed system consists of a
central random number generator that distributes tickets to the participating group,
and their information is stored in a database for easy management. In addition to the
suggested approach, we've developed some business models and revenue distribution
schemes that can generate a high return and provide fair compensation to the
participating group. One possible model is a partnership where the lottery is run
jointly between the state and the participating group, splitting profits 60/40. A
calculation of the annual profit is around $813 million for the Mega Million and
$1.677 billion for the Powerball. Finally, as an alternative, we suggest an
insurance-based model where the participating group can purchase coverage from the
state, and the state can provide financial support to the losing vendors in the event
of a split win. In this model, the annual profit is around $813 million for the Mega
Million and $1.315 billion for the Powerball. Overall, our analysis provides valuable
insights for lotteries with large jackpots and can be useful for future lotteries with
similar characteristics. The proposed collaboration between the state and the
participating group can bring a high return on a lottery ticket,

For operators of a given charge, the mathematical structure of their critical properties can be determined in the weak coupling regime by performing a series of calculations at fixed $Q$. When calculating at the six-loop level, new and complex diagrams that involve five or more legs need to be taken into account - these were previously unencountered in theoretical scalar-field calculations. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. However, this premise doesn't always hold true for real-world data sets, as evidenced by data sets like points on the surface of a sphere that adhere to von Mises-Fisher distributions. In response, researchers have developed adaptations of t-SNE tailored to such non-Euclidean data. While these adaptations have seen limited use, the choice of parameter values often relies on trial and error rather than an informed, hyperparameter-guided approach.

This paper addresses the issue by identifying t-SNE as a curve layman's tool and proposing an adaptation that enables the use of differentiable diffeomorphisms to embed diffeomorphic manifold data. Instead of assuming the diffeomorphic nature of embedded data, the method initializes a diffeomorphism that can be learned and adjusted to produce a more informative embedding. Hyperparameter optimisation using a gradient-based approach is also developed to support the adapted t-SNE algorithm. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm and showcase its application in visualising data from glaucoma patient eyes, surface normals and functions. Additionally, the algorithm is integrated into an interactive, web-based visualization platform that allows for an embedded, informed user experience. As t-SNE is a non-spectral method, the adapted algorithm is an informed, hyperparameter-guided alternative that bridges the gap between t-SNE, Natural Neighbor, and Local Connected Samples. Furthermore, the method's potential for seamless integration into pipelines that utilise t-SDE makes it a viable option, and its implementation as OpenSource is a given. In conclusion, the presented adaptation is a motivated, informed alternative that enables t-SDE to handle a broader range of data types, and as such it should be considered as an inspired version of t-SDE. Similar to t-SDE, the method is available as OpenSource through the provided repository link. In the interest of reproducibility, the experimental results are available at the provided link\@. In the future, further research into the in-place adaptation of t-SDE is warranted, and we anticipate that this work will be the first step in a more comprehensive investigation into the in-place adaptation of t-SDE. In particular, the method is sensitive to the choice of a manifold atlas, and improving the method to automate the creation of the manifold atlas would be beneficial. Leveraging techniques borrowed from image processing, we develop mathematically sound indicators to capture both fine-scale and broad-scale interplay among color categories. We illustrate the utility of these methods by applying them to a variety of multi-modal imaging modalities, including MRI and PET images. In addition to diagnostic applications, our approach also has the potential to provide new insights into cultural heritage artifacts, encompassing objects from prehistoric times to historical relics. Building on Hall, Leung and Li's 2016 model for shared processing multitasking, this research extends the model to a more complex setting with parallel machines by addressing the following questions: What algorithms ensure optimal schedules, and what factors influence task segmentation? How do variations in machine capacity and task requirements impact schedule length? How do factors like processing times and availability of machines affect performance? What is the maximum efficiency gain possible when using parallel machines compared to single machines? Numerical analysis and an optimization algorithm are employed to answer these questions. Findings indicate that machine capacity significantly influences schedule length, while a uniform distribution of machine capabilities generally yields the best results, and optimal schedules can be obtained through a linear programming approach. Furthermore, the study quantifies the difference in performance between parallel machines and single machines, and shows that this difference is primarily influenced by the balance of idle and active machines. Additional machine capacity typically reduces idle machine persistence, eventually eliminating it and resulting in parallel machine performance matching single machine performance in the best case scenario. However, the study also found that adding more machines may extend schedule lengths due to splitting processing steps, and that active idle time parity among machines has a consistent impact on performance, with imbalances causing prolonged processing times. Finally, the largest performance gain from using parallel machines over single machines occurs when single machine processing times are at their highest. All these findings assist in designing strategies to minimize labor costs in service industries using parallel machines. Lastly, the study confirms that without limits on task splitting, optimal schedules may result in single machine utilization, and that this outcome can be mitigated by introducing an additional convex constraint. Moreover, the presence of parallel machines alone does not guarantee the absence of single machine utilization in optimal schedules; however, the inclusion of this extra constraint ensures an efficient schedule with optimal machine cooperation and no single machine utilization. Additionally, the proposed algorithm retrieves the optimal schedule and quantifies the efficiency gain from using parallel machines over single machines, and reveals that this gain is primarily influenced by machine capabilities, while also showing that using more machines generally, though not always, results in reduced processing times. However, the study also found instances where adding machines increased processing times, and that this tends to occur when single machine processing times are high, which lastly reinforces the idea that designing strategies to minimize labor costs in service industries using parallel machines should take into account and manage imbalances among machines. Given the trend towards implementing security measures via codified policy decisions and exchangeable code (like Secure Code Exchange), and with a growing number of devices requiring such updates, we are witnessing an increase in the number of devices seeking these updates concurrently. Unfortunately, this development poses a significant threat to the security and reliability of IoT networks, as simultaneous updates can result in unintended consequences such as rolling updates, where only a subset of devices receive the new code before others are updated. Consequently, there has been limited adoption of this approach. This paper aims to improve the efficiency and resilience of secure codified policy decision mechanisms by introducing a new protocol, known as Policy-Driven Exchange of Codes (PED), which is designed to handle concurrent updates efficiently and minimize the risk of rolling updates. PED achieves this by achieving two key objectives: ensuring concurrent updates are synchronized without delaying updates for individual devices, and securing against potential threats during the exchange process. A case study demonstrates the efficacy and resilience of the proposed PED protocol compared to existing solutions. Comparison results show that PED is capable of processing updates at a rate similar to policy-based solutions for single concurrent updates, while reducing the time required to complete an update when multiple devices seek new code (up to 60%) compared to alternatives like Figure of Merit, Figure of Merit with Confidence Interval, or random policies. Furthermore, the studies exhibit the capability of PED to safeguard against potential threats during the exchange process that previous solutions fail to defend against. Future work can focus on optimizing the design of PED such that it handles extended concurrent updates efficiently and minimizes the time required to complete an update. Comparison results show that PED is capable of processing updates faster than security measures like GMK with policy, GMK with Figure of Merit, or random security measures, with a reduction in time of 60% or more in cases where two or more devices seek new code. A separate study was carried out using real-world IoT devices to experimentally validate the efficacy of the proposed protocol and reveal concealed problems in existing solutions. This was made possible through collaboration with Tennant Instrument, a global company, allowing us to study the behavior of real-world IoT devices using their Pathogen Detection Product. Results show that without synchronization, security measures like GMK with Figure of Merit, random security measures, and policy-based security measures fail to guarantee correct firmware updates for all devices in the network in the face of extended concurrent updates. This failure particularly affects the network when rolling updates

This paper introduces a framework for modeling power system expansion planning with high penetration rates of renewable energy, using a combinatorial optimization approach. We develop an exact solving method based on a factoring technique to tackle large-scale problems. Additionally, the method is enhanced with a technique for removing redundant variables to increase processing efficiency. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we present the results of the method in action on a set of significant case studies. These include real-world data for Germany's power grid and also a stylized model of Australia's power system. These findings reinforce the necessity for utilizing precise and detailed networks when calculating power system expansion planning with high levels of renewable energy, as the results show a substantial distinction between using a detailed model and a simplified model. These findings serve as a motivation for using detailed models and sophisticated algorithms for this type of planning. There is a accompanying video that shows the steps of the method with an example power grid. The video illustrates how the method eliminates redundant variables and factors the model, resulting in processing efficiency improvements. This technique can be applied to any size of power grid and has the potential to be used in other types of power system expansion planning with renewable energy. The technique has been developed into an open-source power system expansion planning with high renewable energy contribution tool, available at https://github.com/Zsarahp/PowerSystemExpansion, which utilises the JuMP optimisation package to solve the model. This tool has been tested on various case studies and is capable of handling up to 8000 variables and 12000 constraints. Furthermore, the tool includes functionality to remove and re-add variables in order to utilise parallel processing for solving large-scale problems. Finally, the results of the method in action on the case studies are presented in a series of figures and tables, resulting in a processing time of 5 minutes for 20 wind farms on an Australiam-sized network and 161 variables and 201 constraints in the base case. The method is capable of being scaled up with the use of parallel processing for any size of power grid and has the potential for further acceleration through the use of faster solvers and further structural reformulation. The open-source code is available at the link above and the specific version used for this study can be downloaded from the following git repository: https://github.com/Zsarahp/PowerSystemExpansion/commit/0d45d09e4f

This phenomenon, which can be measured and characterized, is linked to the formation of micro-cracks within the gel structure, which can either repair or remain intact after the vibrations cease. Moreover, ultrasonic waves significantly reduce the gels' strength against external forces and expedite their transition into a liquid state under stress. Our study paves the way for the manipulation of gel properties and flow behaviors through ultrasonic manipulation, offering exciting avenues for future modeling and exploration of rheo-acoustic materials.

Currently, classification relies heavily on human expertise, but semi-supervised machine learning techniques can aid this process by utilizing labeled data to predict subject categories for previously uncategorized documents. Despite the advancements in semi-supervised learning, practical applications in document subject classification remain challenging due to the limitations of available labeled data sets. This study proposes a refined version of semi-supervised learning that integrates the probabilities from adjacent classes in the hierarchy to predict the subject classifications of documents. , where camera and LiDAR data are combined, is no longer tenable in realistic scenarios due to its vulnerability to LiDAR malfunctions. This has restricted the use of these models in practical autonomous driving applications. Our novel fusion method, called BEVFusion, stands out by not requiring any input from the LiDAR data, thereby addressing this limitation. Our results demonstrate that our method not only surpasses current standards in regular scenarios, but it also outperforms them significantly in environments that mimic real-world LiDAR malfunctions. Specifically, our method shows a substantial gain of 15.7% to 28.7% in terms of mAP when compared to existing solutions. To date, our method remains the first of its kind to tackle real-world LiDAR malfunctions effectively. The code supporting this work is available at https://github.com/ADLab-AutoDrive/BEVFusion. 

Note: BEVFusion is a fusion method that doesn't require LiDAR input. It uses a BEV-MultiView fusion method by processing camera and LiDAR data separately in 2D and 3D domains, then fusing them in the proposal stage with a classification-aware loss function. It can also be used in single-channel input with a simple modification. To address the issue of small object loss during LiDAR malfunctions, BEVFusion uses hierarchical BEV rendering to preserve small objects and enrich context information. It also uses a beam search loss function to combine 2D and 3D detection results, thus enhancing large object accuracy and small object detection. Finally, to address the issue of real-world LiDAR malfunctions, BEVFusion employs adversarial training to improve robustness against LiDAR malfunctions in the training stage. To address the issue of real-world camera malfunctions, BEVFusion uses a simple YOLOv5 3D back-end to combine with the front-end BEVFusion method, thus ensuring robustness against both LiDAR and camera malfunctions in the testing stage.

This paper introduces a novel approach to classify discussion threads as connected to known software issues in a git repository for the Linux kernel, utilizing a combination of machine learning and information retrieval techniques. A two-stage method is presented, which integrates text representation from two fields: the thread title and the body, alongside a network-based technique to account for the threads' relational structure. This method is applied to a large dataset of over 400,000 threads and evaluates its performance alongside alternative models using a balanced training and testing partition. The results demonstrate that a simple title-based model outperforms more complex solutions, including deep learning models and network-based techniques, when tested on a challenging dataset. This suggests that, despite using a straightforward approach, good performance can be achieved given an ample amount of training data, and that the properties of the dataset determine the most effective solution. Consequently, it appears that a simple model is sufficient for identifying issue-related discussion threads in the Linux kernel git repository. This dataset and corresponding code are publicly available.

When encountering questions about new knowledge resources, classes, or properties, these models fall short, making them ineffective beyond their training scope. Leveraging the success achieved in other areas of natural language processing, we developed an innovative approach that involves introducing a mechanism to copy elements directly from questions. Consequently, we recommend using the transformer architecture, combined with the copy mechanism, as the optimal approach for translating English into SPARQL, including when encountering questions about new knowledge resources. ## Overview
The proposed method utilizes the DBLP dataset to develop a quality assessment framework for publishing venues in Computer Science, relying solely on authorship patterns. By employing deep sequential neural networks, this approach is able to discover and accurately evaluate the quality of diverse, previously unknown publishing outlets in comparison to existing methods. Moreover, our method is capable of replicating notable, well-established publishing venues, such as the ACM, IPSJ, and FOCS, with impressive results and substantial improvements over current quality assessments.

To gain a deeper understanding of this AGN's properties, researchers performed the first comprehensive analysis of its XMM-Newton source spectrum and time series. Utilizing advanced models, they achieved better results with two integrated XMM-Newton spectra from two different observations, referencing the host galaxy's luminosity as 3.5 x 10 to the power of 41 erg per second in the 0.2 to 12 keV range and specifying its joint soft and hard X-ray spectrum as a power law with a photon index of 1.98 plus or minus 0.18 coupled with a contribution from the Koruna reflection model. We develop a novel decentralized state observer that integrates local estimates, global communication, and nonlinear correction terms to track disease dynamics accurately. Furthermore, the proposed observer guarantees the continuity of estimated trajectories, which precludes potential divergence in the long term. This solution is showcased on a non-Markovian SIR model with spatial dispersion and variable infectivity, where the observer successfully tracks the global trajectory despite initial errors introduced in specific regions of the system. Our results demonstrate that even with incomplete system information, which fails to satisfy the Markov property, the proposed observer converges to the true system state and supports informed decision-making for disease management. Finally, a general protocol is presented for expanding the concept to more complex epidemic models with multiple nonlinearities and hierarchical dynamics, which are increasingly observed in real-world epidemiological studies. Such modifications could involve super-spreader events in the SIR model, the impact of immunity in the SIR model, multiple nonlinear disease progressions in the SEIR model, and the role of immigrants in the simplified SEIR model. These variations result in locally valid quadratic approximations that require correction as the disease spreads globally, making the proposed observer an effective solution. Nonetheless, the basic structure of the proposed observer remains consistent across these scenarios. Additionally, the proposed observer demonstrates stability and convergence to the true system state with a sufficient sampling period of the communication network, provided that the leakage rate and sampling rate meet specific criteria below the maximum eigenvalue of the system's coefficient matrix A. In practice, the proposed sampling strategy could be enabled through wireless network connectivity, with which the required properties could be established. Additionally, the proposed observer has the potential to be extended into the realm of distributed filtering, where it may lead to the development of more advanced decentralized algorithms than those currently available. This setup reflects varying amounts of non-IID data across participants as well as heterogeneous client engagement influenced by computational and battery limitations. Additionally, the framework accommodates clients joining or leaving at random times and clients occasionally refraining from contributing to training for personal reasons. To alleviate the negative effects of asynchronous client engagement, slow clients can undergo enhanced local training using extra available data to compensate for the increased variance. Notably, the proposed framework does not compromise the model's performance as evidenced by combining classification and segmentation tasks on the CIFAR-10 and CamVid datasets. To automate the process of managing client engagement, we developed an adaptive selection strategy that quickly identifies participating clients and dynamically adjusts the sample size to optimize training efficiency while preventing the best model from being dominated by a small number of high-performing clients. Moreover, we introduced a solution to address the problem of unreliable connection issues between clients and servers. This problem is caused by communication disruptions when users disconnect from the server, which forces the model to be re-synchronized among participants. To prevent this from happening, we developed an algorithm that periodically performs model aggregation only when sufficient participants have contributed to the training process. Moreover, to address the problem of biased model development due to selection bias, we developed a solution that incorporates methods for correcting bias and promoting diversity among participants. This is achieved by calculating a metric indicating the amount of unique contributions from each client and selectively choosing participants with higher values to avoid dominating the training with a small number of clients. The proposed approach was tested on the CIFAR-10 and CamVid datasets and resulted in improved performance compared to traditional stochastic gradient descent. To ensure fair evaluation, we compared our approach to state-of-the-art algorithms like Mini-Batch Edge SGD and APOSDA. The results show that our approach combination is more efficient and robust. We propose the Sparse Structural Network Embedding (SSNE) model, which creates a representation of network nodes suitable for predicting links in these types of sparse networks. Initially, our model converts the network's adjacency matrix into a Sum of Normalized H-order Adjacency Matrix (SNHAM) before passing it through a neural network for a dimensionally-reduced representation. Despite their importance, many of these models struggle to grasp the underlying motivations driving users' actions online, making intent modeling vital for user understanding and optimal long-term behavior forecasting. We've developed a novel approach to probabilistically model user intent using variational autoencoders and inferred latent variables from user behavior signals. Our approach then predicts the next item the user will interact with by minimizing the uncertainty of the intended user intent. We utilize actual user intent ground truth to evaluate our approach and establish a benchmark through experiments on two large-scale production datasets. Our results demonstrate that ours is the first method successfully quantifying user intent from sequential behavior data, significantly reducing uncertainty and enhancing accuracy compared to state-of-the-art models without intent information. Our findings highlight that incorporating intent modeling into sequential models can lead to considerable practical improvements. The corresponding code is available on https://github.com/algebraic/intent_learning. It utilizes variational autoencoders and next item prediction for formulation. From a methodological standpoint, our work indicates that variational autoencoders can effectively uncover unobserved user intent, which can serve as middle-level user representation for enhanced subsequent modeling. The extent of user intent uncertainty directly affects the subsequent item prediction outcome, so modeling and minimizing intent uncertainty may lead to more accurate item prediction. Additionally, our results show that variational autoencoders can successfully capture user intent from behavior signals and aid item prediction in the absence of intent information, making intent modeling using variational autoencoders a promising area for further research. Ultimately, our work may inspire more intent modeling and user characterization in the recommender systems domain. We build upon an existing metric known as the E-value, which measures the reliability of causal inferences, and apply it to scenarios with missing outcome data. Through case studies on Facebook's partially-observed conversion events, we develop an approach for conducting large-scale sensitivity analysis using Bayesian techniques. This approach utilizes a likelihood-based method for inferring data missingness and combines it with iterative steps for estimating the E-value's posterior distribution. We demonstrate that Bayesian sensitivity analysis yields more accurate results than non-parametric estimation methods traditionally used in such scenarios. Additionally, the method can serve as a diagnostic tool for identifying which data missingness scenarios might be most critical. We compare various data missingness patterns in the case studies and conclude that assuming random missingness aligns best with the data's posterior means, while the simplest uniform distribution may not be the best choice due to potential over-conservation in the estimates. The results also show that common testing timeframes might not be sufficient for accurately capturing the E-value's posterior distribution, which highlights the value of regular sensitivity analysis to optimize testing frequency. Our work reveals that conducting large-scale sensitivity analysis can be computationally resource-intensive, which may warrant more efficient algorithms in future research. Finally, the method can be expanded to various performance metrics beyond the E-value, including E-values for specific subgroups and their combinations, extending its applications to metrics such as F-values, union F-values, and the F-Statistic. We showcase the potential of this expansion in the case studies by analyzing union F-values for converting versus non-converting users, demonstrating that conventional testing may underestimate the variability of these metrics and that periodic analysis can provide more accurate estimates with relatively low computational overhead. Furthermore, the partially-converted user is found to be a minor contributor to the overall variability when compared to the non-converting user, which highlights the small risk of conventional testing overlooking essential analytical considerations. Overall, the performed sensitivity analysis reveals that conducting this type of analysis can greatly contribute to making data-driven decisions less uncertain and analysis-driven decisions less dependent on specific assumptions. However, the results also show that conducting large-scale sensitivity analysis may be computationally resource-intensive, which may warrant more efficient algorithms in future research. Furthermore, the type of metric in question may greatly impact the complexity of performing the analysis. We identified specific challenges associated with conducting sensitivity analysis and outlined potential solutions for overcoming these obstacles. This study serves as a starting point for further optimization in the field of performance analysis,

Nevertheless, human requirements often lack essential information, or they contain inaccuracies or ambiguities stemming from written English text. We introduce CitySpec, an innovative AI-powered system for formalizing smart city needs, which effectively bridges language gaps and resolves common data inconsistencies. The purpose of this research is to explain CitySpec's functionality by showcasing three practical applications: real-time requirements completion within CitySpec; a collaborative correction process when unexpected exceptions occur; and the adaptive learning mechanism of CitySpec. Moreover, the paper provides an empirical analysis of formalizing smart city requirements with CitySpec in real-world settings. We present results demonstrating CitySpec's ability to generalize on unseen data and provide an in-depth technical review of its architecture. The full paper, complete with supplementary materials, is available at arXiv:2103.04518. The accompanying video illustrates CitySpec's functionality and supports the paper with additional figures and examples at https://bit.ly/cityspec. By building upon Etter and Ying's '20 elliptic operator shifting framework, we extend this concept to nonsymmetric matrices. Our innovation lies in the development of an operator shifting technique for matrix inverses, which is akin to the James-Stein estimator. This approach entails shifting the estimated inverse matrix in a particular direction to minimize average error. Our research explores the applicability of this technique in the nonsymmetric case, particularly in situations where shifting towards the origin does not always reduce error, unlike in the elliptic case. However, under specific conditions, such as noise symmetry and the use of residual norms as the error metric, we find that the optimal shift remains towards the origin, echoing Etter and Ying's '20 results. Furthermore, we investigate the condition number's impact and discover that a lower threshold exists beyond which the operator shifting technique is unable to improve computation accuracy. Lastly, inspired by the efficacy of our approach in the nonsymmetric case, we adapt this method to tackle the task of matrix inversion, providing an investigation into the optimal way to split the shifted and unshifted components of the estimated matrix inverse, and demonstrating that splitting in a particular direction can lead to improved estimates, especially for small noise levels. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for further investigation into the potential of operator shifting in tackling more complex linear systems inversion problems. In the process, we introduce 'excess eigenvalue' as a novel concept in the field of matrix inversion, which specifically refers to eigenvalues that are above a particular threshold, namely the noise condition number, and we propose that such values pose significant challenges for error reduction using operator shifting. This idea is especially pertinent when dealing with matrices that are ill-conditioned to the extent that noise has a profound impact, and we identify this scenario as another area worthy of further research investigation. In the context of operator shifting, we observe a pattern where'reduction' is often, but not always, associated with the idea of shifting towards the origin, and we seek to explore the conditions under which this association holds, especially in the nonsymmetric case. In the process, we identify correlation as a critical factor in the context of error reduction through operator shifting, and we show that, in cases where two components of the estimated matrix inverse are highly correlated, but the impact of noise is somewhat balanced, shifting towards the origin is indeed the optimal course of action. Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent canonical Hamiltonian systems through a momentum map connection. We outline both an algebraic and a geometric approach to this method, with the latter presented here for the first time. Moreover, we discovered an additional momentum map, resulting in a dual pair of momentum maps, which under specific conditions can represent the process of Lie-Poisson systems collectivization. Consequently, applying symplectic Runge-Kutta methods to solve the system in its canonical form leads to integrators preserving coadjoint orbits and Casimirs precisely. We provide two case studies: the Kida vortex, which corresponds to Lie-Poisson systems on $\mathfrak{so}(2,1)^{*}$, and the heavy top, which corresponds to Lie-Poisson systems on $(\mathfrak{se}(3) \ltimes \mathbb{R}^{3})^{*}$. Additionally, we include the canonical forms of the 1+1 and 1+2 KdV equations as another case study. Our experimental results demonstrate that Clebsch canonization combined with Symplectic Runge-Kutta methods achieves improved long-term integrator precision for Lie-Poisson systems. Our method has been made available through an open-source implementation. This work has been accepted for publication in an upcoming journal. There is no supporting information available for this manuscript. Our method has significant implications for integrator design within the Lie-Poisson framework, leading to enhanced precision when applied to coadjoint orbits. We built upon the recent framework developed by Baks and Heslop integrating Hamiltonian vector fields with a momentum map representation. Under certain data transformations and assuming normal distribution of a dataset, a t-statistic provides an exact p-value; otherwise, the result is an approximation. The p-value can be estimated by analyzing how a sample correlation coefficient behaves under different permutations of the data. Although such estimates may rely on approximations of distribution moments, an inductive approach in this paper offers a precise formula for expressing sample correlation distribution moments in terms of the dataset's central moments, allowing for the development of novel estimation methods to compute the p-value. an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for intricate models that operate as "black-boxes." Recent studies have exposed limitations in local surrogate-based post-hoc explanations regarding their inherent reliability, especially in critical applications such as human-centric recommendation tasks. Moreover, an ideal explanation should enhance key aspects of user experience including clarity and trustworthiness, posing additional challenges to the current approaches. However, a classical post-hoc model utilizing surrogates demonstrates dependence on the model itself, thus falling short in guaranteeing the accuracy of generated explanations. Based on the essential requirement for coherence in explanation output, our new framework addresses these shortcomings and proposes an innovative post-hoc model that seeks solutions outside the model's scope. This framework leverages constraint optimization along with a human-in-the-loop factor to ensure a more effective and efficient solution. Our experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed framework results in more reliable and efficient explanations compared to traditional approaches. Evaluation results indicate a substantial improvement over existing models in achieving transparent and trusted explanations. The framework's source code can be accessed at https://github.com/kim-jongseok/esco. identify ultra-bright Quasi-Stellar Objects (QSOs) located at distant regions of space. By utilizing SkyMapper's DR3, along with 2MASS, VHS, and other datasets, we combine them with accurate positions from Gaia DR2 and eDR3 to create a comprehensive catalog. This catalog contains over 35,000 QSO candidates above a magnitude of 17, with a high precision of 0.1 in terms of their intrinsic brightness. A physical QSO sample is established at a 99% confidence level, featuring 214 objects with a lower bound on their intrinsic brightness of 17.0 and a higher bound of 2.6 billion light years. These QSOs also possess characteristics that are consistent with the broader QSO population. Utilizing this sample, we establish a correlation between the intrinsic brightness of QSOs and cosmic time (L - t) within the redshift range of 0.6 to 2.0 and find that this relationship diverges from the hyperplane established by the average light curve, indicating a variation in the rate at which QSOs decrease in intrinsic brightness over time. This change in the rate may be caused by some QSOs transitioning from high to low and decreasing their intrinsic brightness more rapidly as a result. Additionally, a lack of variation in the shape of the intrinsic brightness of QSOO samples at different redshifts indicates that their black holes have similar characteristics. However, possible deviations from this uniformity may arise at redshifts above 2.5 and below 0.6 due to data limitations. A comparison with the rates of increase in the intrinsic brightness of QSOs, a type of fluctuation, shows that this fluctuation decreases at higher redshifts and could be affected by sampling errors with a high degree of certainty. The lack of variation in the intrinsic brightness of QSOO samples at different redshifts suggests that the intrinsic mechanisms driving supermassive black hole growth are similar at different times, with local universe QPOs potentially serving as a laboratory to study these mechanisms and a wide range of time scales. A possible future study involves analyzing QSOs located near the plane of the Milky Way to establish a more uniform QSO sample. For this purpose, we create a chart listing the necessary observations to identify QSOs located at different distances from the Earth and with varying intrinsic brightness. With these observations, which include data from multiple optical and infrared spectrometers, we can create a comprehensive catalog.

Our contribution is DiffDreamer, an unsupervised system that synthesizes novel long-distance views by simulating camera movements and training on internet-sourced nature scene images alone. Our results confirm that conditioned diffusion models excel at extending long scenes while accurately maintaining both detailed and overall consistency, surpassing prior methods based on GANs. Moreover, in conjunction with prior research on view synthesis, we demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across all evaluation metrics. Our code and data are publicly available. The DiffDreamer system can be easily configured to produce a wide range of creative outputs, such as panoramic scenes, top-down views, and images with desired occlusions, all without any retraining. This capability marks a significant advancement in the field of novel view generation and a promising starting point for future research in automated image manipulation. Our ultimate goal is to develop a system capable of engaging users in interactive, photorealistic virtual tours of distant scenes, similar to existing applications such as Airsim and Google Earth. Moreover, by simulating camera movements and generating consistent views at any distance, we enable a new method of extending partial views to the entire scene, offering novel possibilities for privacy-protection and sentiment-driven image manipulation, where we selectively hide or add objects to the scene based on user-defined preferences or scene context. Our research showcases the significant creative potential of DiffDreamer as a universal image manipulation tool capable of producing photorealistic long-distance views, opening up new avenues for research in the field of novel view generation. This work marks the beginning of a new trajectory in the field of novel view generation, combining the features of GAN-based visual reconstructions, diffusion predictions, and GAN-style manipulations that have previously been explored in isolation. In the future, we plan to extend this approach by integrating user interactions, specifically to leverage prior knowledge and integrate it into the system to produce even more realistic and detailed outputs. Our initial results are a promising starting point for this new direction in research and we are confident that DiffDreamer represents a pioneering development in the field of novel view generation, combining unsupervised learning, long-distance scenes, and user-driven manipulations. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, called the Metric Dimension problem, has been a subject of research since the 1970s. The problem was found to be NP-hard, with parameterization by vertex cover w.r.t. a positive exact exponent. In contrast, parameterization by vertex cover w.r.t. a weighted exponent is completely open. In the present work, we establish that the Metric Dimension problem is $w$-approximable when parameterized by vertex cover, with an improved current best bound of $\mathcal{O}(k^\frac{4}{3})$ decreasing to $\mathcal{O}(k^\frac{2}{3} \log^2 k)$. In addition, we present an NP-complete variant of the problem, where every pair of vertices has at most two distinct shortest paths in common. This variant is known as the $2$-SDMD problem. Finally, with relaxation to the $2$-SDMD problem, we achieve an $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{k}\log n)$-approximation, which still maintains NP-hardness but with less efficient resolution than the standard Metric Dimension problem. In the $2$-SDMD problem, we simulate it as an Induced-Subgraph Problem (I SP), which can be transformed into deleting at most $k$ edges in a complete graph, while still maintaining a resolving set vertices after the transformation. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations. 

By incorporating a clock, with the aid of a clock witness that provides proof of termination at each step using a formula that combines the prior state and the result of the function application, we are able to simplify termination proofs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by providing illustrative examples from the semantics of programming languages, including a simple graph algebra intermediate language, an abstract syntax for JavaScript, and a formalisation of JavaScript dynamics. 

We initially established a set of rules for introducing clocks and making inferences about states, and then showed that using a clock can simplify termination proofs by reducing reliance on fundamental properties of measures that measure state size, effectively providing a syntactic method for proving suitable state sizes using logical formula and avoiding measures that are not easily translated into the logic. This method requires minimal introduction of the clock mechanism, as typically associated with total functions, and instead allows for more natural and context-specific reasoning about termination tailored to the particular property being proven. The proposed technique, dubbed ART, employs transition policy modeling to accurately predict future states and actions using current state information. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavior data, may yield unfair and inaccurate results by neglecting contextual factors. To rectify this issue, we introduce a new assessment method called Expert-centered Driver Assessment. By incorporating expert input from multiple stakeholders in the industry, our approach ensures that the decision-making process is informed by the nuanced interplay between behaviors and environmental conditions. Based on a literature review and expert consultation, we identified crucial factors impacting driving behavior and designed questionnaires for professionals to evaluate. Focusing on two critical contextual elements - road weather conditions and traffic volumes - we collected real-world data and conducted a study to identify their effects on driver behavior. The results confirmed the substantial influence of road conditions and traffic volumes on driver behavior. Using data from our behavioral dataset, we applied a Machine Learning algorithm to create predictive models of driver assessment scores under different weather and traffic conditions. By integrating expert input and contextual data into the models, we increased their predictive accuracy by 18.5% and 15.5%, respectively. Experimental results showed that our Expert-centered Driver Assessment method, combining both behavioral data and contextual factors, provides more accurate and fair evaluations compared to current practices. Furthermore, we increased the predictive accuracy of driver assessment models using our new framework by 11.9% compared to traditional models solely based on behavioral data. By leveraging expert knowledge and incorporating contextual factors, our approach enables more effective assessment and decision-making in the transportation industry. It also lays the groundwork for incorporating other contextual factors, such as urban infrastructure and social environments, to refine the model even further. Ultimately, our framework potentially enables the application of counter-measures to mitigate unfair drivers in the market by suggesting remedial actions based on expert advice. Crucially, we identified areas for future research in driver assessment, providing valuable insights for the development of more robust and accurate models in the field. Finally, by showcasing the practical applicability of our approach in real-world settings, we hope to encourage the adoption of Expert-centered Driver Assessment in the transportation and logistics sector. The framework is openly available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/sagor55/Expert-centered-Driver-Assessment. It demonstrates the feasibility of integrating behavioral data, contextual factors, and expert input to shape decision-making in real-world transportation systems. 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing various languages, domains, and font styles.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising actual OCR predictions, along with correct solutions, to enable quantitative metric assessment.
The competition attracted 52 participants, with 18 submissions received from 9 successful participants, and 32 attempting the secondary track.
The results show that state-of-the-art Neural Network and Convolutional Neural Network models can achieve a precision of approximately 80.6% on normal text and 57.5% on text with curved or tilted font styles.
Furthermore, the challenge's analysis indicates that existing OCR technology is still falling short in handling a substantial proportion (43.7%) of OOV instances that it has never encountered during training. 
Finally, the competition's outcomes and associated code are made publicly available to foster further research on the OOV challenge.

The classic quantum model, formulated by Schrödinger, Heisenberg and Dirac (SDH) in the early 20th century, basically remained the standard for particle description in the mid-20th century. However, its wave-particle representation faced a significant obstacle when trying to explain high-energy particle behavior, particularly in the intense fields of modern particle accelerators and quantum electrodynamics (QED).  In the 1920s, Schrödinger and Dirac attempted to tackle the problem of particle energy using classical action principles, but their efforts did not lead to a general solution.  In the late 20th century, this issue was revisited by a few scientists, including Demkov, Kivshar, Potapov and Smirnov (DPKS) from Russia and Snyder from the US.  The concept of an effective kinetic energy was introduced in the context of the SDH model and was initially used to approximate high-energy particle behavior, but not to understand the physical process.  In contrast, other researchers, including Lehmann, Schwuartz and Thirring (LST) from the 60's tried to describe particle energy using the SDH model with a mathematical transformation, but they did not succeed in establishing a general solution.  In the late 20th century, another attempt was made by Russian researchers Kivshar and Potapov (KP) to address this issue using the SDH model.  In this review, we provide an overview of their work, as well as theoretical developments by other researchers, including Suleimanov and co-authors (SPK), Kim and Yonemura (KY) and Paddison from the US.  In the context of the SDH model, a general solution for high-energy particle behavior in intense fields was achieved by DPKS and KY, however, their work has not been widely recognized when it comes to laser-based applications.  In order to simplify the calculation and achieve a general solution, the concept of an effective action was introduced in the work by DPKS.  This review provides an overview of formal methods, including the effective action, integral transform and instanton, that were developed in the late 20th century to address the theoretical difficulties in explaining high-energy particle behavior, particularly in the intense fields of modern particle accelerators and quantum electrodynamics (QED). For decades, researchers have disputed the underlying cause of the significant entropy change, but this issue is now resolved using a comprehensive approach that incorporates density functional theory-based phonon calculations, inelastic neutron scattering, and additional neutron scattering experiments. In contrast to the previously assumed, albeit widely adopted model of entropy involving disorder across the high-symmetry phase's mirror plane, it is now clear that this simplistic model is invalid. Instead, it is discovered that the significant entropy originates from the low-frequency wobbling of ammonium ions in this phase, which produces small to negligible harmonic components. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for vibrational entropy stemming from broad energy minima, which may be just as significant as configurational entropy due to crystallographic disorder in discovering molecular materials with functional properties. Furthermore, the discovery provides new insights that may empower the design of novel functional materials with broad potential for application. Ultimately, these findings serve as a reminder that in inorganic materials, significant entropy may also arise from vibrational contributions that manifest as apparent disorder, which can be discerned through refined crystallographic analysis. A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. Recent studies propose using artificial intelligence-based techniques but most
methods are one-dimensional as they rely on a single, large dataset, which is
not adaptable. A more effective approach would be for the model to continuously
learn and improve its ability to identify lesion characteristics as it's exposed
to datasets from different hospitals sequentially. We examine the potential of
experience replay, a notable method in the field of artificial intelligence,
specifically within the context of segmenting lesions using images from MRI.
Firstly, we gather data and develop a comparison of recent one-stage deep
learning methods with a new two-stage experience replay method called the
Recurrent Lesion Detector. The results indicate that our new method is
remarkably efficient, achieving impressive accuracy rates of 94.6% in real-world
scenarios compared to previous methods that have reported lower rates of
89.6-91.6%. Moreover, our new method facilitates faster processing, taking
less time to train and evaluate than previous methods by 60% and 30%, respectively.
A further benefit is that our new method automatically identifies distinct patterns
in the data, enabling the segmentation of lesions using images from new, unseen
hospitals without needing extensive retraining. Lastly, our new method's ability
to accumulate experience over time allows it to continuously improve its ability
to identify MS lesions regardless of the hospital or dataset in question. 
In general, our new method outperforms previous methods in various areas, such
as detecting new lesions, identifying boundary irregularities, and enhancing
overall lesion detection. The code used to develop this paper has been made
publicly available at a specified GitHub site. The study's underlying code has
been made publicly available at https://github.com/acarnell19/MS-Lesion-Detector.

creating predictive models for complex systems using data, two examples being traffic models and a typical supply chain model. These systems comprise interconnected components where state transitions in each component influence other parts, leading to aggregate effects. For such complex systems, there's a challenge in determining the time it takes for individual local changes to be fully reflected in measurable system outcomes. This delay is referred to as the aggregate behavior generation time. In a typical setting where data is limited and incomplete, it's not feasible to accurately estimate this delay through mathematical means. Therefore, a statistical approach is developed to estimate the aggregate behavior generation time from a limited number of observations. By assuming that local changes follow a particular pattern and that variations around this pattern are random and unique, we can link this characteristic to a function that can be calculated directly from observed data. A method based on this connection is presented along with recommendations on choosing a suitable function. The proposed method is tested in models representing the dynamics of interconnected components, using synthetic and real-world data, and it's demonstrated to be as effective as a method that requires complete knowledge of the underlying system model, a typical setting where data is complete. Moreover, the method has the potential to be applied to a broader range of problems involving dynamical systems, the details of which are presented in the paper. By extending the concept of collective behavior generation time to a dynamic setting, we can estimate this time even when the system model is changing over time. This is based on an assumption that local changes remain the same during successive periods of stability. By applying statistical analysis to determine when variations occur, we can identify when new stability is achieved. A practical demonstration of this concept is shown in a model representing the dynamics of following behavior in a group of vehicles. Through various tests, it's shown that the statistical method is as effective as a method with complete knowledge of the underlying system model, a typical setting where data is complete. This is based on an assumption of local changes having similar effects during successive periods of stability. The proposed method has practical potential in various fields, starting with applications to models representing simple vehicle behavior on roads and models representing the dynamics of following behavior in a group of vehicles.

Specifically, when a new edge is added, it follows the preferential attachment rule with a certain probability and otherwise forms between two randomly selected nodes.  This approach leads to a distribution of node in- and out-degrees that has more moderate characteristics compared to purely preferential or uniform attachment networks. Both the single and double hybrid network models can facilitate efficient and fast computations of key network properties in various time complexities.  The double hybrid network has the potential to improve upon the stochastic block model in several aspects: eliminating unnecessary edge structures, refining degree distribution clustering, increasing clustering quality, and reducing computation time while also offering easier data collection and interpretation.  Both the single and double hybrid network models can be utilized for a variety of applications, such as network analysis, simulation, and random graph generation with properties tailored for a specific purpose. Overview
------- 

Gravitational influences on quantum systems are subject to diverse interpretations, although a detailed examination of related effects is still lacking in the literature. This study specifically focuses on understanding how the gravitational forces affect particles with mass dependent on location,  placed within a universe with defects like cosmic strings and space-time dislocations. Gravitational Effects on Quantum Systems Moving at Varying Speeds
---------------------------------------------------------

When studying the impact of gravitational forces on quantum systems, we start by considering the simplest case - a particle with mass dependent on location in a universe without the feature of cosmic strings. The Schrödinger equation for this particle reveals that its wave function is influenced by its velocity. However, this effect disappears when considering the impact of the gravitational forces on the particle's potential. 

On the other hand, when a rotating particle is taken into account, its velocity and angular speed contribute equally to its wave function. Furthermore, as the particle continues to rotate, its wave function becomes influenced by its angular momentum, due to the increase in velocity based on its mass, which in turn affects its rotation speed.

However, test code can be compromised by suboptimal design or implementation choices referred to as test smells. These shortcomings can significantly undermine the quality of software systems by exacerbating difficulties in comprehension, amplifying maintenance complexities, and making systems more susceptible to bugs and errors. Prior studies have investigated the likely consequences of test smells on test code. Despite their focus, a knowledge gap remains regarding the perspectives of developers regarding these issues. To fill this knowledge gap, a study empirically examined how software developers perceive the level of impact test smells have on test code. The research analyzed the perspectives of developers from six open-source projects, inquiring about the influence test smells have on test code and whether they consider it a pressing concern. The results indicate that while developers often view test smells as minor concerns within their own projects, they recognize the potential for significant negative consequences when asked more generally. The current study provides the first empirical validation that the concerns regarding test smells expressed in previous studies originate, to a considerable extent, from the concerns and opinions of developers themselves. The prevailing subspace randomized methods used for tensor decompositions have a critical flaw: they don't adapt the data passes number (q) in response to the inherent rank of the tensor. If the inherent rank is significantly smaller than the total number of data passes (q), this approach results in superfluous computations. In order to resolve this issue, we introduce an optimized method for calculating t-SVD in a limited number of data passes. This approach not only minimizes additional computation based on an estimate of the inherent rank, but also internally updates and refines this estimate as needed. As a result, we achieve faster computational speed while maintaining accuracy. Additionally, we present a randomized algorithm for computing t-KLT in the HRMRF framework, utilizing a lower number of data passes (q). The method involves performing t-SVD with (q/2)-data passes and employing the positive semidefinite factorization of the transformed tensor for further computation, resulting in a decreased error bound that is linearly related to the estimated inherent rank. In cases where the estimated inherent rank is significantly smaller than (q/2), this yields an optimal error bound, equal to the one obtained with full data passes. Furthermore, we present numerical results illustrating the proposed method's performance advantages. This method is also applicable to other HRMRF algorithms, including total least squares and regularized tensor hypercontractivity. In line with our proposed method, we present an optimized algorithm for regularized tensor hypercontractivity with internal data pass adaptation, resulting in a faster and more robust method for tensor rank-revealing factorization. This method is then utilized in a new regularization approach for tensor completion. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed approach results in improved performance, especially for incomplete and noisy tensors. The method has been developed into an open-source code available on GitHub at the provided link. The code enables the user to perform t-SVD in (q \times p)-data passes (with p \leq 3) while estimating the inherent rank and specifying the error bound, staying within data memory bounds. In addition to the proposed methods, we introduce the first comprehensive open-source library focused solely on randomized tensor decompositions, named PyrandTensor, available at the provided link. This library includes the proposed methods as well as other novel approaches for tensor decomposition and is built upon Python 3 and the cuRAND library

We formally define dynamic graph embedding and categorize it into problem settings and a novel taxonomy of input and output. We also discuss different dynamic phenomena and categorize them according to topological changes, feature evolution, and network processes. In addition, existing methods and a classification of algorithmic approaches, ranging from matrix factorization to deep learning, random walks, temporal processes, and reinforcement learning, are presented. Furthermore, this survey links research on dynamic graph embedding with foundational work in network analytics and showcases applications of this area. Lastly, this survey outlines prominent challenges and suggests future research directions. We hope this survey serves as a comprehensive reference for researchers and practitioners in dynamic graph embedding. All related source code and data will be publicly available upon release. Additionally, a supplementary website providing additional resources and links to existing works is provided at https://dynamicge.net. We intend to update this website and code regularly to ensure their continuity. We conclude this survey by highlighting ongoing and new research projects and initiatives related to dynamic graph embedding, such as the AMEN initiative and the SEMMS project. We welcome the participation of new members to further advance this area. Finally, this survey concludes with a tribute to the memory of Dr. Loda-Antonio, a close friend and colleague, who passed away in 2020. We will always remember his kindness and enthusiasm for dynamic graph embedding. We are proud to have him as a reference in our work. Following the initial completion of this survey in 2020, we have made significant efforts to expand it to cover more existing works and develop new content related to this topic. We have now integrated around 1600 words of new content, increased the total length of our survey by nearly 60%, and provided over 200 new citations to existing works in this area. We have also detailed the implementation of five dynamic graph embedding algorithms and provided open-source code for these methods. Moreover, we have created and released open-source datasets, including topics such as network description, node features, and embedding

Current approaches for addressing this issue often involve leveraging pre-intervention patterns to forecast post-intervention outcomes, often assuming a group's past behavior is representative of the broader population. We propose a more sophisticated method that allows for modeling the divergence between individual and collective trends over time, thereby enabling more accurate group-level impact assessments. This novel method has been effectively applied in analyzing the media's influence on public perception of science and technology, revealing that influential media outlets exceed the impact of their ordinary followers. Additionally, our method's utility in detecting intentional disinformation effects is demonstrated through an investigation into the perceived success of Twitter's fact-checking initiative. We establish that, aside from a brief initial adaptation, the media's role in shaping public perception remains superior to that of the platform's users. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only eye-motion data and a single image capture, thereby making the camera calibration process more streamlined. Specifically, our approach involves generating a three-dimensional point from the captured image and minimizing distance between this point and the hand's position, all while being trained using synthetic data and fine-tuned on real-world data. When compared with existing methods, our approach demonstrated improved accuracy, especially in situations with low saturation levels of the captured image. Furthermore, our results indicate that focusing specifically on hand movement yields more accurate results than considering the entire eye-motion data. Additionally, we analyzed existing depth estimation methods and proposed a novel approach for depth estimation in scenarios with low image saturation. This proposal involves combining multiple models and weighing them according to the image's saturation level. In conclusion, our approach and other methods were evaluated on two datasets and showed promising results, laying the groundwork for future research in robotics-based eye-in-hand camera calibration. The method involves collecting data on the bull's eye devices while gradually disconnecting part of its inner section. The proposed experimental setup affords the application of the cut-and-identify technique in conjunction with a more comprehensive set of measurements, referred to as the central cross, to pinpoint Majorana mode. Furthermore, among the various possible explanations for observed suppression of coherent readings in central cross measurements, competition between pairs of confined states in the outer ring is considered the most plausible one. As such, it is possible to eliminate non-Majorana origin of zero-energy peaks through simple physical experimentation and analysis. In specific cases where the action space has a constant Hessian and the expected regret is sub-linear in the number of steps, we show that the minimum eigenvalue grows with $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ for large $n$. In contrast to previously observed logarithmic growth, these "locally rich" action spaces force polynomial growth, effectively shifting the analysis towards a polynomial rather than a logarithmic lower bound. Notably, unlike the previous result, which was proven asymptotically as $n \to \infty$, this result holds at any point in time. Moreover, under a mild technical assumption, we obtain a lower bound with high probability. To further demonstrate the practical implications of our finding, we show that our spectral bound is particularly useful for tackling real-world challenges, such as model selection and clustering, in the context of linear bandits. In model selection, we leverage our spectral bound to derive sharp finite-sample bounds for estimating model complexity using the Spectral Penalty method introduced in Arbel et al. (2020), resulting in improved performance at a linear convergence rate. In this research, a comprehensive dataset of binding energies for ice and gas phases has been developed with enhanced resolution, which includes previously unstudied molecular motifs. This novel dataset is distinct from existing references and corrects prevailing shortcomings, such as inaccurately represented low-energy interactions and the excessive presence of ice-specific binding energies for larger molecular complexes. To address research questions regarding the dynamics of molecular complexes, a straightforward and efficient neural network implementation has been developed to estimate binding energy values within $0.1$ kmol per km square parsec density regimes. This neural network is initially trained on datasets using centrally aligned frames of reference and then adapted for use in generally aligned frames of reference. Notably, when this research calculated $0.1$ kmol per km square parsec collisional probabilities for a selection of molecules, it found that while the results from both reference frames matched in terms of top 10 results, there were substantial differences in estimated probabilities for middle-tier molecules. This discrepancy highlights the requirement for improved precision in binding energy calculations for understanding the impact of thermal destruction rates on molecular evolution. Finally, a web-based tool has been created to facilitate research into a range of unexplored regimes, including higher densities and a broader array of molecular complexes and temperature regimes. This research is available online at with accompanying code available through GitHub under the same reference. In addition, a series of collisionally induced changes to ice structures and compositions have been proposed on the basis of an exploration of the relevant physics, which are outlined in further detail within the referenced paper. This paper presents a probabilistic model, Probability of Peak Demand (PoPD), designed to forecast the probability of each household and group of households experiencing peak demand, by factorizing probabilistic loads into individual household probabilistic loads. The prevailing method in the field of deep learning constructs matching cost through the sequential shifting of each sub-aperture image with predefined offsets, making the process intricate and labor-intensive. This paper proposes a novel cost constructor, designed with convolutional neural networks, to efficiently generate matching cost for light field depth estimation. Our constructor, leveraging specifically engineered dilation rates, seamlessly combines pixels under predetermined disparities without any shifting, thereby ensuring a faster processing time. The proposed constructor also possesses occlusion-aware properties, enabling the dynamic modulation of pixels from different views and the effective handling of occlusions. By incorporating this innovative constructor, a deep learning-based light field depth estimation network has been developed, yielding the top results in the MSE category on the standard 4D LF benchmark, as well as on the LLFF benchmark, and performing competitively while processing images at a significantly faster rate than the existing state-of-the-art methods. The proposed constructor is highly adaptable and can be readily integrated into other light field depth estimation networks to further optimize their performance and processing speed. Code for the proposed constructor is available on GitHub at https://github.com/rydygier/LFDConstr. The results of our experiments are presented in the supplementary materials. The proposed cost constructor bears similarities with cost aggregators in stereo matching, but we currently do not have a unified understanding of this relationship. Our paper is the first to systematically introduce this concept in the context of deep learning. As such, we have formulated the problem of designing a cost constructor for matching cost with the formulation $E_{CC} = \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_p \cdot S_p(x_i)$, with subscripts denoting individual pixels $x_i$ with neighbors $p$, $i$, and $n$, and coefficients $\alpha$ that are pixel weight and loss function compatible. Our paper is the first to employ this formulation and employs an element-wise multiplication to effectively model loss for individual pixels. Additionally, we have introduced a multi-channel representation of a cost constructor, enabling the construction of matching cost with various disparity gradients, an aspect that current methods lack. The proposed cost constructor is the first deep learning approach that seamlessly integrates a sophisticated matching cost with a convolutional neural network, without necessitating any shifting and making the processing much faster than existing methods. The increasing use of high-bandwidth applications such as online gaming, virtual reality, and high-definition video streaming require networks with enhanced throughput levels and reduced latency. One effective strategy for achieving these goals is to use multiple access technologies in unlicensed frequency bands. This study examines the potential of mesh-Wi-Fi networks as a promising solution, analyzing their performance characteristics and offering practical advice for optimizing them in real-world applications. To this end, we introduce and evaluate a novel backhaul routing protocol that takes into account the network's changing topologies and non-deterministic delays to ensure efficient path selection.
